nodes.text: The matrix separates cognitive and affective empathy, sympathy, and compassion, then profiles psychopath, sociopath, empath, altruist, and integrated ideal.

evidence.text: Legend: check mark = present / defining; tilde = partial / possible; blank = absent / not required.

The four component columns (cognitive and affective empathy, sympathy, compassion) sit left of the double rule. The five to the right are whole-person profiles, arranged darkest to lightest: psychopath, sociopath, empath, altruist, and the integrated ideal. Rows stay ordered by the two dark profiles' contrast, in four blocks separated by blank dividers: present in both, in the psychopath only, in the sociopath only, and in neither.

Note 6: the psychopath is close to the cognitive-empathy column standing alone; the sociopath is close to the affective-empathy and sympathy columns clamped to a narrow in-group and stripped of regulation; almost everything the psychopath has, the sociopath also has in degraded form, so cold instrumental control is the psychopath's one distinguishing possession.

Note 9: terminology varies across literature (empathic concern, Brown-style sympathy). Note 10: the five profile columns are ideal types on a dark-to-light spectrum; empath is not the moral ideal; altruist matches the Light Triad (Kaufman et al., 2019); integrated ideal alone scores well across every block. Note 11: the three Light Triad rows partly restate earlier rows; only Faith in Humanity adds a new dimension.

nodes.text: Cognitive empathy means accurate modeling, boundary, and control; it survives in manipulators.

evidence.text: Block present-in-both plus psychopath-only rows. Accurately modeling the other's mental state: cognitive check, affective partial, sympathy partial, compassion check; Psychopath check, Sociopath partial, Empath partial, Altruist check, Integrated check. Maintains self/other boundary: cognitive check, sympathy check, compassion check; Psychopath check, Sociopath partial, Altruist check, Integrated check. Can exist in manipulators / con artists: cognitive check only; Psychopath check, Sociopath partial. Controlled / instrumental rather than reactive / impulsive: cognitive check, sympathy partial, compassion check; Psychopath check, Altruist check, Integrated check.

Note 1: Sympathy gets tilde on modeling the other's mind because you can pity someone while badly misreading them. Note 2: Affective empathy gets tilde on capacity to care: contagion can happen involuntarily, without real concern. Note 3: The manipulators row is the sharpest diagnostic for the cognitive/affective split and the psychopath's signature; cognitive empathy alone is compatible with cruelty.

evidence.text: Block sociopath-only rows. Actually sharing / mirroring the emotion: affective check; Sociopath partial, Empath check, Altruist partial, Integrated check. Motivation to help or act: affective partial, sympathy partial, compassion check; Sociopath partial, Empath partial, Altruist check, Integrated check. Produces guilt / remorse after causing harm: affective partial, sympathy partial, compassion partial; Sociopath partial, Empath check, Integrated partial. Risk of emotional contagion and burnout: affective check, sympathy partial; Sociopath partial, Empath check, Integrated partial. Biased toward vivid, similar individuals: cognitive partial, affective check, sympathy partial; Sociopath check, Empath check, Integrated partial. Treats people as ends, not means (Kantianism): affective partial, sympathy partial, compassion check; Sociopath partial, Empath check, Altruist check, Integrated check. Values each person's dignity and worth (Humanism): affective partial, sympathy check, compassion check; Sociopath partial, Empath check, Altruist check, Integrated check.

Note 4: The sustainable and scalable row reflects the Bloom/Singer argument (Paul Bloom, Against Empathy, and Tania Singer's compassion-training research), which is a position, not a consensus; critics reply compassion without empathic grounding risks becoming abstract or paternalistic. Note 5: Boundary maintenance is the structural difference between affective empathy and everything else: merging drives its power, burnout, and bias.
